title: Weekends Can Restore, But They Don't Do It On Autopilot: Here Are Two Simple Practices That Can Help ple-practices-that-can-help
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that weekends don't automatically restore a person the way many teachers assume — 'weekending well' is a practiced art and craft requiring the same intentionality that structures the workweek. He offers two concrete practices for making rest actually restorative: twenty minutes of silence in nature without earbuds or phones, framed as achievable alone, with a child, or with a spouse; and the 24-Hour Challenge, a stretch (usually Saturday evening to Sunday evening in his household) during which work of any kind — email, grading, planning — simply doesn't happen. He traces the 24-Hour Challenge to the ancient Jewish practice of Shabbat, which he and his wife observe as an expression of their Christian faith, and is candid that they don't always succeed at the full 24 hours, treating lapses as data rather than failure. The piece frames disciplined rest as essential to sustaining a teaching career for the long haul rather than as an indulgence competing with professional excellence.
points: Rest during a wired, always-on era is a skill that requires deliberate practice, not something that happens automatically once free time appears on the calendar.
Twenty minutes of phone-free silence in nature is framed as an accessible entry point to restorative rest, adaptable for solo use, with a child, or with a spouse.
The 24-Hour Challenge — a full day with zero work contact, rooted in the Jewish practice of Shabbat — deliberately interrupts the belief that the world depends on one's constant performance.
Treating lapses in a rest practice ('we sneak a peek at email') as observable data rather than moral failure keeps the practice sustainable over time instead of provoking all-or-nothing abandonment.
quotes: Which of the things or people I say "Yes" to and which of the things or people I say "No" to is of critical import — my very life, and the lives of those to whom I most owe my love, will be determined by the sum of my yes or no decisions.

I'm starting to learn that weekend is a verb and an art and a craft. Weekending well — in a way that restores me and my family for the week to come — takes practice, intentionality, study, and inquiry.

Find a trail or a park or a backyard near where you live, and go there to sit or walk for twenty minutes. No earbuds, no phones. Your goal is to be quiet amidst other things that are A) alive and B) unable to make demands on you.

The idea is simple: for 24 hours straight, you don't read or think or write or check email about work. You don't do paper stacks, you don't do mindless grading while watching a movie — work just doesn't exist for those 24 hours.
For go-getters like Crystal and me, what we're most challenged and restored by in the 24 hours is the idea that the world doesn't depend on our performance or our keeping up with things.

Regardless of your philosophical bent, may I strongly recommend the 24-Hour Challenge to you, too. It is such a good practice for those of us educators who want to maximize the long-term flourishing outcomes of our classrooms while not sacrificing our lives on the altar of professional success.
